```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

DietView makes few assumptions about your data: one row per prey record, a
predator column, a stomach column and a prey key. Everything else is declared.
This article goes through the choices you make when you bring a survey of your
own, in the order you meet them. The worked example is the public ICES stomach
data that ship with the package (ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES,
Copenhagen; extract distributed with the R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026;
see `?ices_diet`): a real survey export, with its own column names and codes,
that was not designed for DietView.

```{r setup}
library(DietView)
```

## 1. Map your columns

Start from the table as you have it. `ices_diet` keeps the column names of the
stomachr extract:

```{r columns}
names(ices_diet)
```

Then decide which column plays which role. Your table keeps its own column
names; `dv_spec()` only records the mapping:

| Role | ICES column | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `predator` | `predator_common` | a display label; `predator_aphia_id` or `predator_latin` would do as well |
| `predator_latin` | `predator_latin` | used for the species cards |
| `stomach` | `stomach_id` | must be unique across the whole table |
| `prey_id` | `prey_aphia_id` | the WoRMS AphiaID, `NA` for unidentified material |
| `prey_name` | `prey_name` | the scientific name, used when there is no ID |
| `weight` | `prey_weight_g` | grams |
| `count` | `prey_count` | individuals per record, for %N |
| `digestion` | `digestion_stage` or a label built from it | see below |
| `covariates` | `region`, `year`, `quarter`, ... | anything you will compare across |

Survey exports usually need a few decisions before the mapping is complete.
The ICES data need four.

**The stomach identifier.** It must be unique across the whole table, not only
within a predator, a haul or a year: stomach counts (frequency of occurrence,
aggregation thresholds, matrices) count distinct identifiers, so two stomachs
that share an identifier count as one. Check it:

```{r stomach-id}
pred_per_stomach <- tapply(ices_diet$predator_common, ices_diet$stomach_id,
                           function(z) length(unique(z)))
table(pred_per_stomach)
hauls_per_stomach <- tapply(ices_diet$haul_id, ices_diet$stomach_id,
                            function(z) length(unique(z)))
table(hauls_per_stomach)
```

Each ICES stomach belongs to one predator and one haul. If your identifiers
restart in each haul or each year, build a unique one first, for example
`mydata$stom <- paste(mydata$haul_id, mydata$fish_no, sep = "_")`. A related
case: `r sum(tapply(ices_diet$n_fish_pooled, ices_diet$stomach_id, function(z) any(z %in% 2)))`
stomach samples in `ices_diet` pool two fish (`n_fish_pooled == 2`). They are one
identifier and are counted as one stomach; say so, or drop them.

**What counts as diet.** The export lists everything found in the stomach:

```{r item-types}
table(ices_diet$item_type)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
sum(phylum %in% "Nematoda")
```

Non-food items (sand, stones, plastic) are not diet. Nematodes in fish
stomachs are mostly parasites. Unidentified material is diet whose taxon is
unknown, and it stays. DietView does not filter for you; the documentation
drops the first two:

```{r filter}
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]
```

**Digestion codes.** ICES reports the digestion stage as a code (0, 1, 2),
missing for many records. You can declare the code column directly
(`digestion = "digestion_stage"`), but the missing stages then appear as an
`NA` group in `dv_digestion_diagnostic()`, easy to confuse with unidentified
prey, and a bare code is hard to read in a table. The
bundled data carry a label column built like this:

```{r digestion}
lab <- c("0" = "0 pristine", "1" = "1 affected", "2" = "2 skeletal remains")
dl  <- unname(lab[as.character(dat$digestion_stage)])
dl[is.na(dl)] <- "not recorded"
identical(dl, dat$digestion_label)
table(dl)
```

The labels are inferred from the older ICES format, whose three classes match
the shares of codes 0, 1 and 2; check them against the ICES vocabulary before
you rely on them. "not recorded" keeps the records without a stage in the
table as a group of their own.

**Units.** Check them before anything else, against the survey documentation
and against the values. When the bundled data were built, two unit errors in
the predator variables were fixed (Belgian lengths reported in mm, Danish
weights in kg). A quick look at the range of each numeric column per country
catches most of them:

```{r units}
round(sapply(split(dat$length_cm, dat$country), max, na.rm = TRUE))
```

With those decisions made, declare and validate:

```{r spec, message = TRUE}
spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",
  prey_name      = "prey_name",
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter")
)
dv_validate(dat, spec)
```

Give both a prey ID and a prey name when you have them: the ID is used for the
lookup, and the name lets DietView check that the two agree. In the ICES data
every identified prey has an AphiaID; the
`r format(sum(is.na(dat$prey_aphia_id)), big.mark = ",")` records without one
are the unidentified material.

## 2. Attach a taxonomy you can check

With `taxonomy = "worms"`, DietView looks each distinct prey up in the World
Register of Marine Species and keeps a log of how it was matched. Read that log
before you use the result:

```{r worms, eval = FALSE}
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "worms")
dv_taxonomy_report(prep)   # the matches that need a look, largest first
```

For the ICES data that means `r length(unique(stats::na.omit(dat$prey_aphia_id)))`
lookups by AphiaID, plus one by name for "Unidentified material", which is
expected to stay unresolved. Each prey gets a `match_type`:

| `match_type` | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | The AphiaID is accepted in WoRMS | Nothing, unless `name_check` is `"differs"` |
| `id_synonym` | The AphiaID is unaccepted; its accepted ID was used | Check that the accepted name is the taxon you meant |
| `id_unchecked` | WoRMS could not be reached to check the ID | Run again later |
| `exact` | No ID; the name matched exactly | Nothing |
| `fuzzy` | No ID; the name was matched by TAXAMATCH, which tolerates misspellings | Check every one: a near match can be a different taxon |
| `unresolved` | No match | Correct the name, or accept that the prey stays unidentified |

A `name_check` of `"differs"` means the name in your table is not the name
WoRMS holds for that AphiaID: either the ID or the name was mistyped. A
`lineage_ok` of `FALSE` means the prey was matched but its classification
could not be retrieved; its records count as unidentified until you run the
lookup again. Fix what the report lists, then save the lineage.

## 3. Freeze the taxonomy for the analysis

WoRMS changes. For an analysis you will publish, resolve the taxonomy once,
save it as a lineage table, and run every later step from that file.
`ices_lineage` is such a table:

```{r lineage}
dim(ices_lineage)
ices_lineage[ices_lineage$scientific_name %in% c("Crangon crangon", "Crustacea", "Pisces"), ]
```

It has one row per AphiaID, a key column named like the `prey_id` column of
the data (`prey_aphia_id`), and one column per rank; an empty cell means the
prey was not identified to that rank. `scientific_name` and `worms_rank` are
kept for the reader and ignored by DietView.

Freezing your own takes two lines after a WoRMS run, and the frozen table
gives exactly the same result offline. Here, starting from a prepared object:

```{r freeze}
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)

keep <- !is.na(prep$data$prey_aphia_id)
lineage <- unique(prep$data[keep, c("prey_aphia_id", prep$ranks)])
nrow(lineage)

f <- file.path(tempdir(), "lineage_2026-10-20.csv")
write.csv(lineage, f, row.names = FALSE)

lineage2 <- read.csv(f, na.strings = c("NA", ""))
prep2 <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = lineage2,
                    verbose = FALSE)
identical(dv_tree(prep), dv_tree(prep2))
```

This path needs neither `worrms` nor a network connection, and it gives the
same result every time it is run on the same files. Archive the lineage table
with your data and record the date it was retrieved. A prey that is missing
from the lineage table, or a key that appears twice, triggers a warning or an
error instead of passing unnoticed:

```{r freeze-missing, warning = TRUE}
crangon <- ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id[ices_lineage$scientific_name == "Crangon crangon"]
prep3 <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table",
                    lineage = lineage2[lineage2$prey_aphia_id != crangon, ],
                    verbose = FALSE)
```

If you build the lineage table by hand, for example for prey outside WoRMS,
take the classification from one stated authority and cite it.

## 4. Choose the ranks

By default DietView shows seven ranks, kingdom to species. Pass `ranks` to
show others; every rank you list must be a column of the lineage table:

```{r ranks}
spec5 <- dv_spec(predator = "predator_common", stomach = "stomach_id",
                 prey_id = "prey_aphia_id", prey_name = "prey_name",
                 weight = "prey_weight_g",
                 ranks = c("phylum", "class", "order", "family", "genus"))
prep5 <- dv_prepare(dat, spec5, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                    verbose = FALSE)
c(seven_ranks = nrow(dv_tree(prep)), five_ranks = nrow(dv_tree(prep5)))
```

Rank names are WoRMS rank names in lower case, so on the WoRMS path
intermediate ranks such as `"subclass"` or `"infraorder"` can be added. A
frozen table holds only the ranks it was built with: `ices_lineage` has the
seven default ones, so adding `"infraorder"` (which would separate crabs from
shrimps inside Decapoda) means going back to WoRMS once and freezing again.

Fewer ranks make a simpler figure, but they also merge information: without
`"species"`, a prey named to species and one named only to its genus look the
same. Check one more thing on your own prey list: some taxa have no entry at
one of the requested ranks in WoRMS. Such a prey shows an unidentified node at
that rank with named taxa beyond it, and that node then mixes prey that were
not identified with prey that were identified but have no taxon at that rank.
Find those nodes before you report an unidentified share:

```{r na-with-children}
tree <- dv_tree(prep)
named_kids <- tapply(tree$label != "NA", tree$parent, any)
holes <- tree[tree$label == "NA" & tree$id %in% names(named_kids)[named_kids], ]
holes[, c("id", "rank", "value_occ")]
```

In the ICES data these are the polychaetes, whose unidentified order node
holds `r holes$value_occ[grepl("Polychaeta", holes$id)]` records, some of them
in families that WoRMS places in no order; a lancelet (Leptocardii) with a
family but no order; and Priapulida, which have no class. Their `NA` rows in
`dv_rank_table()` at that rank are not all unidentified prey.

## 5. Colors

`dv_palette()` gives each name a color and unidentified nodes white. Build it
from the names in your own data rather than typing them:

```{r colors}
pal <- dv_palette(prep$data$class)
length(pal)
head(pal, 6)
```

Pass the result to `dv_sunburst(colors = pal)`. To give one taxon a color of
your choice, change that element: `pal[["Malacostraca"]] <- "#1f77b4"`. The
palette has 20 colors and reuses them after that. With several hundred taxa,
as here, `dv_palette_tree(tree)` is the better choice: one hue per phylum,
tints below it.

## 6. Periods and length classes

Add a covariate column, list it in `dv_spec(covariates = )`, and build periods
and length bins with the helpers:

```{r cov}
table(dat$year)
dv_add_period(c(2020, 2022, 2023, 2024), breaks = c(2019, 2022, 2024))
dv_size_bins(c(15, 20, 34, 58), breaks = c(0, 20, 35, 50, 110))
```

A year on an inner break goes to the earlier period (2022 above), and a length
on an inner break goes to the bin that starts there (20 cm above). Values
outside the breaks get no level. The ICES years are very uneven, so choose
breaks from the table of years, not from round numbers. The article on
covariates shows how to compare diets across the levels.

## 7. Freshwater, terrestrial and mixed prey

WoRMS covers marine taxa and many brackish and freshwater ones. When DietView
matches a name without an ID, it restricts the search to marine records, so a
strictly freshwater or terrestrial prey named without an AphiaID will often be
`unresolved`. For such prey, build a lineage table from an authority that
covers them (for example GBIF or the Catalogue of Life) and use
`taxonomy = "table"` (section 3). If your prey list mixes marine and other
taxa, resolve the marine part with WoRMS, append the rest by hand from the
other authority, and say in your methods which authority supplied which part.
